description_full: Home BancShares, Inc. operates as the bank holding company for Centennial Bank that provides commercial and retail banking, and related financial services to businesses, real estate developers and investors, individuals, and municipalities in the United States. The company offers deposit services, including checking, savings, and money market accounts, as well as certificates of deposit. It also provides loans comprising non-farm/non-residential real estate, construction/land development, residential mortgage, consumer, agricultural, and commercial and industrial loans. In addition, the company offers other banking services, such as internet and mobile banking, voice response information, cash management, overdraft protection, direct deposit, and automatic account transfer services, as well as safe deposit boxes and the United States savings bonds. Further, it provides trust, wealth management, and custodial services, as well as trustee services, escrow, and paying agent services. Additionally, the company writes policies for commercial and personal lines of business, including insurance for property, casualty, life, health, and employee benefits. It operates its branches in Arkansas, Florida, Texas, South Alabama, and New York City. Home BancShares, Inc. was founded in 1903 and is headquartered in Conway, Arkansas.
ceo_bio: Mr. John W. Allison | Co-Founder, Chairman & CEO | Age 78 | Compensation: $2.5M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 2K people. Revenue per employee of $429K ranks in the below the sector median among Financial Services peers, improving at 14%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $148K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $4K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 6× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags moderate compensation governance risk (6/10).
financial_summary: Home BancShares, Inc. is a mid-cap financial services business with a $5.9B market cap on $1.1B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +5% over the past three years and +10% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 14% against a 8% cost of capital, a 5-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $377M in free cash flow — roughly 35 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, with adequate 0.84× cash conversion.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin 1.6× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 4.1% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 6.4% of the shares, and within its sector the business captures 2.2× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Altman Z in the distress zone (0.5) — the kind of balance-sheet risk that can make a loss permanent
Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Above-average short interest at 6.7% of float
Insiders are overwhelmingly selling (89% sell ratio) — the people who know the business want less of it
Late-cycle dynamics increase the probability of a slowdown
Credit cycles and regulatory capital — losses accumulate invisibly in good years and appear all at once, and the time to worry is when underwriting standards are loosest.
Fintech disintermediation — neobanks, embedded finance, and blockchain rails are unbundling the fee streams that traditional banks took for granted.
Interest rate regime shifts — a rapid move in rates can invert the yield curve, crush bond portfolios, and trigger deposit flight simultaneously.

sector_tailwinds: Operating margins 27% above sector median — the quantitative trace of pricing power
Shares offer a 26% margin of safety against estimated fair value
Market is pricing in lower growth than the company has historically delivered
Founder-led — owner alignment that often matters more than any incentive plan
19 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment

sect: Its 56% operating margin runs 27pp above the Financial Services median (29%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.16x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+4.7% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.02 across 512 companies in the universe; the top four hold 20% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 9% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 6% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 20% and a beta of 0.75, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.17 vs 5y 0.70), so read it loosely.
About $42.7M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 50% in the 2020 crash, 21% in the 2022 bear market and 53% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 26% below its DCF fair value of $40.42, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 16%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $33.08 to $51.44 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
The EBIT multiple is close to its own 10-year median (-4%).
The 8 covering analysts target $32.75 on average, 10% above the price.
The price implies 1.2% annual cash-flow growth, 6pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 14% earns above the cost of capital of 8.5%, but the 5pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.34).
It converts 35% of revenue into free cash flow.
As a lender it runs a net interest margin of 4.62% and an efficiency ratio of 41% (lean).
It earns a 11% return on equity.
hlth: CET1 capital of 14.8% sits comfortably above the ~7% regulatory minimum with buffer.
Non-performing loans are 0.55% of the book, a clean credit profile.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 5.3% over 3 years, 9.5% over 5 years and 10.0% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 13%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 2.1% on average.
Analysts expect 2.7% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own 6.4%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 80%.
Insider trading is two-way: 1 purchase and 8 sales over the past year, net $107K bought.
It returns 4.1% a year to shareholders (1.4% in buybacks and 2.9% in dividends).
The share count has grown 4.0% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It has paid a dividend for 19 consecutive years, raising it 12.6% a year over the last five.
people: With about 2,543 employees, each generates about $429K of revenue, in line with the Financial Services median, and productivity has risen 13.6% a year.
That works out to $148K of free cash flow per employee.
The company is founder-led, which often keeps management aligned with long-term owners.
CEO pay is $2.5M (6x revenue per employee).

profile.head: Watch: no strong case either way.
